Rattanakosin Era 112

May it long stand in the reign.

Preface.

May there be prosperity. The Buddhist Era, having passed through its bygone periods, now stands at 2431 years, at the present time, in the Year of the Rat, the month of Māgha, the dark fortnight, the first day, a Saturday — this being the appointed time.

His Majesty King Paramindr Maha Chulalongkorn, Bodindhara Thepaya Mahamongkut, Burushayaratana Rajaravivongse, Varutama Phongsa Boriphat, Vara Khattiya Rajanikarodom, Chaturanta Boromo Mahachakkraphat Rajasangkat, Boromo Dhammika Maharajadhiraja, Boromo Nart Bophit, King Chulalongkorn —

graciously considered that the entirety of the Buddha's teachings, which the sons of good families have studied and practiced up to this day, are entirely contained within the Pali Canon (the Tipitaka). In former times, kings who revered the Buddhist religion would, out of royal faith, act as patrons of the religion, giving support to the monks, the disciples of the Buddha, so that they might hold councils to purify...

Introduction.

The Pali Tipitaka scriptures, time after time, have been handed down as a royal tradition, and have been inscribed in letters on palm leaves as copies transcribed one from another, thus becoming editions widely disseminated throughout all the countries that revere the Buddhist religion. In former times, the countries that revered the Buddhist religion still had the power to govern themselves independently, with the monarch, who was a devotee of the Buddhist religion, nurturing and supporting the religion. This occurred in several countries together, namely: the Kingdom of Siam, the land of Lanka (Ceylon), the land of Burma, the land of Laos, and the land of Cambodia. Whenever calamity or danger arose and the Tipitaka was lost or became incomplete in any country, people could rely on borrowing from one another to recopy and keep the text complete, passing it back and forth between each other.

But in the present day, the countries of Lanka and Burma have fallen under the power of England. Those who govern and administer these lands do not revere the Buddhist religion; they merely look after the people and citizens of the land, but do not support the Buddhist religion the way that monarchs who revered Buddhism did in former times. The monks who follow the Buddhist teachings each act according to their own individual ways. Since, as is natural, those who are bad outnumber those who are good, this leads the scriptural teachings of the Fully Enlightened Buddha to become corrupted and distorted according to personal inclination. As for Cambodia, it too has fallen under the power of the French, and lacks the strength to support the Buddhist religion in a stable and lasting way. As for Laos, which lies within the royal territory of Siam, though the nobles and the common people there do revere the Buddhist religion, it has become corrupted and confused through mixing with spirits and deities, so that it cannot be taken as a firm and reliable foundation. If the Tipitaka should become corrupted and altered at this time, there would no longer be any means of verification and recopying as there was in former times. Thus the matter of the Buddhist religion...

PREFACE

Because His Majesty held the royal opinion that it would be more beneficial than inscribing on palm-leaf manuscripts - printing once could yield many hundreds of copies, which could be picked up and carried about without difficulty, and those wishing to examine and verify them could do so easily, since the text of one scripture would all be gathered together in a single volume, not scattered about or incomplete. Even though paper may not be as durable and lasting as palm leaves - which is true - still, one printing produces many times more copies than inscribing on palm leaves, tens of times more. And if kept and cared for properly, it can last a long time, counted in hundreds of years. Whenever any edition becomes greatly needed, it can be printed again in even greater quantity, and more quickly than it could be inscribed on palm leaves. Thus the scriptures of the Dhamma would spread and become complete throughout the Kingdom of Siam for the future. Seeing this benefit, His Majesty therefore formed the royal wish to print the Dhamma scriptures so as to make them widespread, as a support for the firm establishment of the teachings of the Fully Enlightened Buddha for the future.

Furthermore, regarding this royal wish to print the Dhamma scriptures at this time: His Majesty's heart was set on hoping it could be completed in time to meet the date he had fixed in his royal heart - namely, that if he should remain on the royal throne for twenty-five years, he would have a grand celebration held in honor of this Tipitaka, as an act of royal merit on that auspicious occasion. Whether or not he would remain on the throne until that appointed time could naturally not be taken as certain. But His Majesty considered that this undertaking - to examine, verify, and have the Tipitaka produced and spread widely - would be of benefit to all people in general, and could be reckoned a great act of royal merit, being in accordance with righteousness, and would surely serve to support the fulfillment of the Royal wish.

Therefore a Royal Command was graciously given, commanding His Royal Highness the Prince, younger brother of the King...

Preface.

Prince Bhanurangsi Savangwongse, of the Department of Bhanubandhuvongse Varadej, served as the head
in charge of arranging the printing of the Tipitaka, and by royal command had the responsible officials invite
the royal princes who had been ordained as monks, together with the ecclesiastical dignitaries, titled monks, and learned scholars of
the Pali scriptures, to gather and deliberate according to the royal intention and purpose. They then
divided among themselves the work of examining and correcting the original texts before sending them to be printed, and the work was completed in full accordance with
the royal wish.

He dedicated the merit arising from this undertaking of having the Pali scriptures created
on this occasion to all people everywhere, wishing that this Pali scripture, now printed and established,
may endure and remain for a long time to come.

Reading stanzas.

The Buddha, utterly pure, a vast ocean of compassion,
whose eye of knowledge perceives the completely pure and excellent truth,
the destroyer of the world's sin and defilement —
I worship that Buddha with devotion.

The Dhamma, like a lamp for that Teacher,
which is distinguished by the attainment of path and fruit,
transcendent, and which illuminates that very goal —
I worship that Dhamma with devotion.

The Sangha, regarded as a field more excellent than a good field (of merit),
which has seen peace and follows after the Well-Gone One (the Buddha) in awakening,

The Noble One, free from restlessness, the wise one —
I reverently worship the Sangha with devotion.

Thus, having composed this verse of homage to the Triple Gem,
which is worthy of utmost veneration,

by the merit that I have gained,
may all misfortunes of mine

never arise,
through the power of its accomplishment.

In the Sutta Piṭaka, the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

The Khuddakapāṭha

The Going for Refuge.

I go to the Buddha for refuge. I go to the Dhamma for refuge. I go to the Saṅgha for refuge.
For the second time, I go to the Buddha for refuge. For the second time, I go to the Dhamma for refuge.
For the second time, I go to the Saṅgha for refuge. For the third time, I go to the Buddha for refuge.
For the third time, I go to the Dhamma for refuge. For the third time, I go to the Saṅgha for refuge.

Here ends the Going for Refuge.

The Khuddakapāṭha: The Ten Precepts.

I undertake the precept to abstain from taking life. I undertake the precept to abstain from
taking what is not given. I undertake the precept to abstain from unchastity.
I undertake the precept to abstain from false speech. I undertake the precept to abstain from
fermented and distilled liquors which are the basis for heedlessness. I undertake the precept to abstain from eating at improper times...

1. The Three Refuges.

In the Sutta Pitaka, the Minor Collection (Khuddaka Nikaya).

...I undertake the training rule. I undertake the training rule to abstain from watching dancing, singing, music, and theatrical shows.
I undertake the training rule to abstain from wearing garlands, using perfumes, and adorning or beautifying oneself with ointments.
I undertake the training rule to abstain from using high and luxurious beds and seats.
I undertake the training rule to abstain from accepting gold and silver.

The Ten Training Rules are finished.

From the Khuddakapatha: The Thirty-two Parts of the Body.

In this body there are: head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs; intestines, mesentery, stomach-contents, feces; bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, urine; and in the head, the brain.

The Thirty-two Parts are finished.

From the Khuddakapatha: The Novice's Questions.

What is called "one"? All beings subsist on food. What is called "two"? Name and form. What is called "three"? The three kinds of feeling. What is called "four"? The four noble truths. What is called "five"? The five aggregates subject to clinging. What is called "six"? The six internal sense-bases. What is called "seven"? The seven factors of enlightenment. What is called "eight"? The noble eightfold path. What is called "nine"? The nine abodes of beings. What is called "ten"? One who possesses ten qualities is called an Arahant.

The Novice's Questions are finished.

Sutta Pitaka, Khuddaka Nikaya.

"Timely discussion of the Dhamma — this is the highest blessing.
Austerity and the holy life, and the seeing of the Noble Truths —
and the realization of Nibbana — this is the highest blessing.
One whose mind, though touched by the ways of the world, does not waver,
being sorrowless, stainless, and secure — this is the highest blessing.
Having accomplished such things, everywhere unconquered,
everywhere they go in safety — that for them is the highest blessing."

Thus ends the Mangala Sutta.

The Ratana Sutta, from the Khuddakapatha.

"Whatever beings are gathered here,
whether of the earth or in the sky,
may all beings be of happy mind,
and let them listen carefully to what is said.
Therefore, O beings, all of you give heed,
show loving-kindness to the race of humans
who by day and night bring offerings;
therefore guard them, being heedful.
Whatever treasure there is, here or beyond,
or whatever excellent jewel in the heavens,
there is none equal to the Tathagata.
This excellent jewel is in the Buddha.
By this truth, may there be safety.
[The excellent jewel of] the ending, the fading away, and the deathless..."

Khuddakapāṭha: The Ratana Sutta (The Jewel Discourse)

That which the Sage of the Sakyas, concentrated, attained —
there is nothing equal to that truth;
this too is a sublime jewel in the Dhamma.
By this truth, may there be safety.

That which the excellent Buddha praised as pure,
which they call "concentration with immediate fruit" —
there is nothing equal to that concentration;
this too is a sublime jewel in the Dhamma.
By this truth, may there be safety.

The persons praised by the good as the eight,
who make up these four pairs —
they, the disciples of the Well-farer, worthy of offerings,
what is given to them bears great fruit;
this too is a sublime jewel in the Sangha.
By this truth, may there be safety.

Those who, well applied with firm mind,
without longing, in the Teaching of Gotama,
having attained what is to be attained, having plunged into the deathless,
having freely obtained peace, enjoying it;
this too is a sublime jewel in the Sangha.
By this truth, may there be safety.

Just as a boundary-post fixed firmly in the earth
could not be shaken by the four winds,
so too do I declare the true person who...

In the Sutta Pitaka, the Khuddaka Nikaya.

They clearly perceive the noble truths,
This too is a precious jewel in the Sangha.
By this truth, may there be well-being.

They who clearly understand the noble truths
Well taught by the one of deep wisdom —
However heedless they may yet be,
They will not take up an eighth existence.
This too is a precious jewel in the Sangha.
By this truth, may there be well-being.

Together with the attainment of insight,
Three things come to be abandoned:
Identity-view, and doubt,
And whatever clinging to mere rules and vows there may be.
Being fully freed from the four states of woe,
One is incapable of committing the six great wrongs.
This too is a precious jewel in the Sangha.
By this truth, may there be well-being.

Whatever evil deed such a one may do,
By body, by speech, or by mind,
He is incapable of concealing it;
Such incapability is declared of one who has seen the path.
This too is a precious jewel in the Sangha.
By this truth, may there be well-being.

Just as a grove of flowering trees...

In the Suttanta Pitaka, the Khuddaka Nikaya.
Whether in the realms of earth or those of the sky—
I pay constant homage to the Tathagata, honored by gods and men.
May there be well-being.
Here ends the Ratana Sutta.

The Khuddakapatha and the Tirokudda Kanda.

If, by giving up a trifling pleasure,
One sees that abundant happiness may be gained,
Let the wise one forsake the trifling pleasure,
Having regard for the abundant happiness.

They stand outside the walls,
At crossroads and junctions;
They stand beside the doorposts,
Having returned to their former homes.

But when food and drink are abundantly set out,
Both hard and soft foods prepared,
No one remembers them,
Because of the nature of their past deeds.

Thus those who feel compassion
Give to their departed kin
Food and drink that is pure, excellent, and timely, and proper,
Saying: "May this be for our relatives; may our kinsfolk be happy!"

And those who have gathered there—
The departed relatives assembled together—
When food and drink are abundant,
Respectfully express their gratitude:

"May our relatives live long,
Because of whom we have received this;
Honor has been shown to us,
And the givers are not without reward."

For there is no farming there,
Nor is cattle-herding to be found;
There is no trade such as exists here,
No buying and selling with money.

Those who have died and passed on
Live there on what is given from here,
Just as water that rains upon the heights
Flows down and settles in the hollows—

Even so, what is given from here
Reaches and benefits the departed.

From the Khuddakapatha: The Tirokudda Kanda.

As rivers full of water, flowing on,
fill up the ocean to the brim,
even so does what is given here
benefit the departed ones.

"He gave to me, he did for me,
he was my kinsman, friend, companion" —
remembering such things done before,
one should give an offering for the departed.

For neither weeping, nor grief,
nor any other kind of lamenting
helps the departed in any way;
thus do their relatives merely stand by.

But this offering, when given
and well established in the Sangha,
works for their lasting welfare
and benefits them at once.

Thus has this duty toward kinsmen been shown,
great honor has been paid to the departed,
strength has been given to the monks,
and no small merit has been produced by you.

Here ends the Tirokudda Kanda.

From the Khuddakapatha: The Chapter on the Treasure

A person buries a treasure
in a deep place near the water,
thinking: "It will serve my purpose
when some need or business arises --
to free myself from a king's anger,
or if oppressed by thieves,
to pay off a debt,
or in time of famine or misfortune" --
for such purposes in this world
is a treasure buried.
Though it is thus well hidden
in a deep place near the water,
it does not always
serve all his purposes:
the treasure may shift from its place,
or his memory of it may fail,
or nagas may carry it away,
or spirits may take it off,
or unloved heirs
may dig it up when he is not looking --
when his store of merit is exhausted,
all of this is lost.

But for one who, through giving, through virtue,
through restraint and self-control,
has well hidden a treasure --
whether that person be a woman or a man --
hidden in a shrine, in the Sangha,
in an individual, in a guest,
in a mother, in a father,
or in an elder brother --

this is a treasure well hidden,
it cannot be taken away, it follows him;
leaving behind all that must be left behind,
he takes this treasure along when he goes.

It is not shared with others,
no thief can carry it off;
let the wise one perform meritorious deeds --
this is the treasure that follows one.

This is the treasure that grants all wishes
to gods and to human beings;
whatever gods and humans aspire to,
all of it is obtained through this.

Beauty of complexion, sweetness of voice,
fine bodily form, handsome appearance...

[Page number: 12]

The Khuddakapāṭha: The Discourse on Loving-Kindness (Karaṇīya Metta Sutta)

This is what should be done by one who is skilled in goodness, and who knows the path of peace: let one be able and upright, straightforward and gentle in speech, humble and not conceited, contented and easy to support, unburdened with duties and simple in livelihood; with senses calmed, and discreet, not bold or greedy among families.

Let one not do the slightest thing that wise people would later censure. [Thinking:] "May all beings be happy and secure, may their hearts be at ease!"

Whatever living beings there may be — whether weak or strong, without exception, long or large, medium, short, subtle or gross,

seen or unseen, those living far or near, those already born or those yet to be born — may all beings be happy at heart!

Let no one deceive another, nor despise anyone anywhere. Let no one wish harm to another out of anger or resentment.

Just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so too should one cultivate a boundless heart toward all living beings:

radiating thoughts of loving-kindness over the entire world — above, below, and across — without obstruction, without hatred, without enmity.

Whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, as long as one is free from drowsiness, one should be firmly established in this mindfulness. This, they say, is the sublime abiding here and now.

Not adopting wrong views, endowed with virtue and vision, having removed greed for sensual pleasures, one will surely not come again to lie in a womb.

Here ends the Metta Sutta.
The Khuddakapāṭha is concluded.

The Verses of the Dhammapada.

The Chapter of the Pairs.

Mind precedes all mental states; mind is their chief, they are all mind-made.
If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind,
suffering follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the cart.

Mind precedes all mental states; mind is their chief, they are all mind-made.
If one speaks or acts with a pure mind,
happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves.

"He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me" —
those who harbor such thoughts do not let go of their hatred.

"He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me" —
those who do not harbor such thoughts let go of their hatred.

For hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world...

The Yamaka Chapter.

He rejoices here, he rejoices hereafter,     having seen the purity of his own deeds.
Here one suffers, and hereafter one suffers;     the evildoer suffers in both places,
Thinking "I have done evil," he suffers;     he suffers even more when gone to a bad destination.
Here one rejoices, and hereafter one rejoices;     the one who has done merit rejoices in both places,
Thinking "I have done merit," he rejoices;     he rejoices even more when gone to a good destination.

Even if a man recites much of the sacred texts,
but, being heedless, does not act accordingly,
like a cowherd counting the cows of others,
he has no share in the fruits of the holy life.
Even if a man recites but little of the sacred texts,
but lives in accordance with the Dhamma,
having abandoned passion, hatred, and delusion,
possessed of right knowledge, with mind well freed,
clinging to nothing here or hereafter,
he has a share in the fruits of the holy life.

The Yamaka Chapter, the first.

The Chapter on Heedfulness.

Heedfulness is the path to the deathless,     heedlessness is the path to death.
The heedful do not die,     the heedless are as if already dead.
Having clearly understood this distinction,     the wise, being heedful,
rejoice in heedfulness,     delighting in the domain of the Noble Ones.
They, being meditative, persevering,     always firm in their effort,
the wise attain Nibbana,     the supreme rest from bondage.

From the Sutta Piṭaka, the Khuddaka Nikāya.

The glory of one who is energetic, mindful,
pure in action, considerate,
restrained, and who lives by the Dhamma,
and who is heedful, grows ever greater.

By effort, by heedfulness,
by discipline and self-control,
let the wise one build an island
that no flood can overwhelm.

Fools and unwise people
give themselves over to heedlessness,
but the wise guard heedfulness
as their greatest treasure.

Do not give yourselves to heedlessness,
nor to intimacy with sensual delight;
for the heedful one, absorbed in meditation,
attains abundant happiness.

When the wise one, through heedfulness,
drives away heedlessness,
having climbed the terrace of wisdom,
free from sorrow, he looks upon the sorrowing multitude—
like one standing on a mountain
looking down upon those on the plain below.

Heedful among the heedless,
wide awake among the sleeping,
the wise man advances
like a swift horse leaving behind a weak one.

By heedfulness, Maghavā (Indra)
attained the highest place among the gods;
heedfulness is praised,
heedlessness is always blamed.

A monk who delights in heedfulness,
who sees danger in heedlessness,
advances burning away all fetters,
great and small, like a fire.

A monk who delights in heedfulness,

This matter was spoken by the Blessed One. And in connection with this it is said:

    "In a single aeon, the heap of bones of one person,
    if gathered, would be a pile as high as a mountain" - so said the Great Seer.
    This indeed is what is called the great Vepulla mountain,
    higher than Vulture's Peak, in the mountain-enclosure of the Magadhas -
    by which one sees with proper wisdom the noble truths:
    suffering, the arising of suffering, and the overcoming of suffering,
    and the noble eightfold path leading to the calming of suffering.
    That person, having wandered on at most seven more times,
    makes an end of suffering, through the destruction of all fetters.

This too is a meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One, thus have I heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, thus have I heard: "Monks, for a person who has transgressed one thing, I say there is no evil deed that he would not do. What is that one thing? Monks, it is this: deliberate lying." This matter was spoken by the Blessed One. And in connection with this it is said:

    "For one who has transgressed the one thing - a liar,
    one who has gone beyond [concern for] the next world -
    there is no evil he would not do."

This too is a meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One, thus have I heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, thus have I heard: "Monks, if beings knew, as I know, the result of sharing in giving, they would not eat without having given..."

Itivuttaka, Collection of Ones, Third Chapter. 197

...they would eat, and the stain of selfishness would not overpower and remain fixed in their minds; and even if it were their last morsel, their very last mouthful, they would not eat it without sharing, if there were someone to receive it. But because, monks, beings do not know, as I know, the result of sharing in giving, therefore they eat without giving, and the stain of selfishness overpowers and remains fixed in their minds. This matter was spoken by the Blessed One. Here it is said:

"If beings knew, as declared by the Great Sage,
the result of sharing, how it brings great fruit,
having dispelled the stain of selfishness with a clear and confident mind,
they would give in due season to the noble ones, where what is given bears great fruit.
Having given food to many, and offerings to those worthy of offerings,
passing on from this human state, the givers go to heaven.
And having gone to heaven, they rejoice there, their desires fulfilled,
they enjoy the fruit of sharing, being free from selfishness."

This too is the meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Whatever grounds there are, monks, for making merit connected with the substrata of existence — all of them are not worth a sixteenth part of the mind-release through loving-kindness; the mind-release through loving-kindness alone, having surpassed them, shines, burns, and blazes forth. Just as, monks, whatever light there may be from the forms of the stars, all of it is not worth a sixteenth part of the moon's light; the moon's light alone, having surpassed them, shines, burns, and blazes forth. Even so, monks, whatever grounds there are for making merit connected with the substrata of existence, all of them are not worth a sixteenth part of the mind-release through loving-kindness; the mind-release through loving-kindness alone..."

In the Itivuttaka, the Third Chapter of the Section of Ones.

...they do not amount to a sixteenth part
(as moonlight is to a host of stars).

One who does not kill nor cause killing,
does not conquer nor cause conquest,
being full of loving-kindness toward all beings,
has no enmity with anyone.

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One — so I have heard.

The Third Chapter, the third.

Its summary:

Mind, radiance, both kinds of benefit,
merit, the vow of growth,
deliberate false speech,
giving and the development of loving-kindness,
seven discourses,
and twenty before them —
discourses on single qualities,
twenty-seven in all, gathered together.

Thus ends the Section of Ones.

In the Itivuttaka, the First Chapter of the Section of Twos.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, possessed of two qualities a monk dwells in suffering in this very life, with vexation, with despair, with distress; and at the breaking up of the body after death, a bad destination is to be expected. What two? Not guarding the doors of the sense faculties, and immoderation in eating. Possessed of these two qualities, monks, a monk dwells in suffering in this very life, with vexation, with despair, with distress, and at the breaking up of the body..."

[One should] expect a bad destination after death. This is the meaning that the Blessed One spoke. And in this connection it is said:

"Eye and ear, nose as well, tongue, body, and mind too -
these are the doors of a monk that are unguarded;
not knowing moderation in food, unrestrained in the senses,
he experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
With body burning and mind burning,
whether by day or by night, such a one dwells in suffering."

This too is the meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, possessed of six qualities, a monk dwells happily in this very life, free from distress, free from despair, free from fever, and at the breaking up of the body after death a good destination is to be expected. Which six? Guarding the doors of the senses, and moderation in eating. Monks, possessed of these six qualities, a monk dwells happily in this very life, free from distress, free from despair, free from fever, and at the breaking up of the body after death a good destination is to be expected." This is the meaning that the Blessed One spoke. And in this connection it is said:

"Eye and ear, nose as well, tongue, body, and mind too -
these are the doors of a monk that are well guarded;
knowing moderation in food, restrained in the senses,
he experiences bodily happiness and mental happiness.
With body not burning and mind not burning,
whether by day or by night, such a one dwells in happiness."

This too is the meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

Itivuttaka, Dukkanipāta - First Chapter. 201

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, there are these two things that torment. What two? Here, monks, a certain person has not done good, has not done wholesome deeds, has not made himself a refuge against fear, has done evil, has done cruelty, has done wickedness. He is tormented, thinking, 'I have not done good,' and he is tormented, thinking, 'I have done evil.' These, monks, are the two tormenting things." This is the meaning the Blessed One stated. And in this connection it is said:

"Having done bodily misconduct, and verbal misconduct too,
Having done mental misconduct, and whatever else is connected with fault,
Not having done wholesome deeds, but having done much that is unwholesome,
At the breaking up of the body, the unwise one is reborn in hell."

This too is the meaning stated by the Blessed One; so I have heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, there are these two things that do not torment. What two? Here, monks, a certain person has done good, has done wholesome deeds, has made himself a refuge against fear, has not done evil, has not done cruelty, has not done wickedness. He is not tormented, thinking, 'I have done good,' and he is not tormented, thinking, 'I have not done evil.' These, monks, are the two things that do not torment." This is the meaning the Blessed One stated. And in this connection it is said:

"Having abandoned bodily misconduct, and verbal misconduct too,
Having abandoned mental misconduct, and whatever else is connected with fault,
Not having done unwholesome deeds, but having done much that is wholesome,
At the breaking up of the body, the wise one is reborn in heaven."

This too is the meaning stated by the Blessed One; so I have heard.

     "With evil conduct and wrong view,
     A person endowed with these two things,
     At the breaking up of the body, being unwise,
     Is reborn in hell."

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One; so I have heard.

Thus was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Bhikkhus, a person endowed with two qualities is cast into heaven, as if brought and placed there. What two? Good conduct and right view. Bhikkhus, a person endowed with these two qualities is cast into heaven, as if brought and placed there." This meaning was spoken by the Blessed One, and so it is said:

     "With good conduct and right view,
     A person endowed with these two things,
     At the breaking up of the body, being wise,
     Is reborn in heaven."

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One; so I have heard.

Thus was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Bhikkhus, a monk who is without ardor and without moral shame is incapable of awakening, incapable of Nibbana, incapable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage. But, bhikkhus, a monk who is ardent and has moral shame is capable of awakening, capable of Nibbana, capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage." This meaning was spoken by the Blessed One, and so it is said:

Itivuttaka, Chapter of Twos, First Chapter. 203

One who is without ardor, without a sense of shame, lazy, of inferior energy,
Who is full of sloth and torpor, shameless and uncaring —
Such a monk is incapable of touching the supreme enlightenment.

But one who is mindful, wise, and meditative,
Ardent, conscientious, and heedful,
Having cut the fetter that leads to birth and aging,
Touches the unsurpassed enlightenment right here.

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One, thus have I heard.

Thus was it said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "This holy life, monks, is not lived for the purpose of deceiving people, nor for the purpose of flattering people, nor for the sake of gain, honor, and praise, nor so that people may think of me in a certain way. Rather, monks, this holy life is lived for the purpose of restraint and for the purpose of abandonment." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke. Thus it is said:

The holy life, not mere hearsay, for the purpose of restraint and abandonment —
This the Blessed One taught, leading to the plunge into Nibbana.
This is the path followed by the great and wise sages;
Whoever practices it, just as taught by the Buddha,
Will make an end of suffering, being doers of the Teacher's instruction.

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One, thus have I heard.

Thus was it said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "This holy life, monks, is not lived for the purpose of deceiving people, nor for the purpose of flattering people, nor for the sake of gain, honor, and praise, nor so that people may think of me in a certain way. Rather, monks, this holy life is lived for the purpose of direct knowledge and for the purpose of full understanding." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke. Thus it is said

204          In the Sutta Piṭaka, the Khuddaka Nikāya.

The Blessed One taught the incomparable holy life (brahmacariya) of higher knowledge and full understanding, leading to the plunge into Nibbāna; this is the path followed by the great ones endowed with great wisdom. Those who practice it just as it was taught by the Buddha will put an end to suffering, having carried out the Teacher's dispensation.

This too is a meaning spoken by the Blessed One — thus have I heard.

Thus was it said by the Blessed One, said by the Worthy One, so I have heard: "Monks, possessed of two qualities a monk dwells happily and joyfully in this very life, and sets out rightly for the destruction of the taints. What two? Being moved by a sense of urgency (saṁvega) in matters that call for it, and by right striving born of that very urgency. Possessed of these two qualities, monks, a monk dwells happily and joyfully in this very life, and sets out rightly for the destruction of the taints." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke. And on this it is said:

"In matters calling for a sense of urgency, let the wise one be stirred;
An ardent, discerning monk, having examined well with wisdom,
Dwelling thus — ardent, of calm conduct, not restless,
Devoted to the stilling of the mind — attains the destruction of suffering."

This too is a meaning spoken by the Blessed One — thus have I heard.

The First Chapter, the First [section].
Its summary:

These two are what burn a monk: austerity, and burning on account of others;
Being ardent and without deceit, and with joy — these are [the two things].

206		Sutta Pitaka, Khuddaka Nikaya.

That sage, bearer of his final body,
who has left Mara behind, I call one gone beyond old age;
just as one standing on a mountain peak
can see the people below all around,
so too, the wise one of all-seeing wisdom,
having climbed the palace made of Dhamma,
himself free from sorrow, looks down
upon people sunk in grief, overcome by birth and old age.

This too is a meaning spoken by the Blessed One, thus have I heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, thus have I heard: "Monks, there are two kinds of Dhamma teaching that the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, gives by way of method. What are the two? 'See evil as evil' — this is the first Dhamma teaching. 'Having seen evil as evil, become disenchanted with it, become dispassionate toward it, be released from it' — this is the second Dhamma teaching. Monks, these are the two Dhamma teachings that the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, gives by way of method."

This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke. And on this it is said:

"Of the Tathagata, the Buddha,
compassionate to all beings,
behold this teaching given by method —
two Dhammas have been proclaimed:
See evil, you wise ones,
and toward it become dispassionate;
then, with minds grown dispassionate,
you will make an end of suffering."

This too is a meaning spoken by the Blessed One, thus have I heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, thus have I heard: "Monks, ignorance is the forerunner for the arising of unwholesome states, followed closely by shamelessness and lack of moral dread. And knowledge, monks, is the forerunner for wholesome states..."

In the Itivuttaka, of the Twos (Duka-nipāta), the Second Chapter.                    207

"...attainment, together with moral shame and moral dread." This is the meaning that the Blessed One spoke. Thus it was said:

"Whatever bad destinations there are,
In this world and in the next,
All are rooted in ignorance,
Piled up by craving and greed.

Since one who has evil wishes,
Who is shameless and uncaring,
Thereby produces evil,
And by that goes to a woeful state.

Therefore, dispelling desire and greed,
And ignorance as well,
A monk, generating true knowledge,
Abandons all bad destinations."

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

Thus was this said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, those beings are greatly deprived who are deprived of noble wisdom: they dwell in suffering even here and now, with distress, with despair, with torment; and with the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected. Monks, those beings are not deprived who are not deprived of noble wisdom: they dwell in happiness even here and now, without distress, without despair, without torment; and with the breakup of the body, after death, a good destination is to be expected." This is the meaning that the Blessed One spoke. Thus it was said:

"By the loss of wisdom,
See the world together with its gods,
Settled upon name-and-form,
Thinking, 'This is true.'

Wisdom indeed is the foremost thing in the world,
That which leads to penetration,
By which one rightly understands
The ending of birth and existence.

Them — both gods and humans —
The Fully Awakened Ones, the mindful,
Those of joyful wisdom,
Bearers of their final body —
These are longed for."

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

Thus was this said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "These two, monks..."

208                    Sutta Piṭaka, Khuddaka Nikāya

Bright (wholesome) qualities protect the world. Which two? Shame and fear of wrongdoing. If, monks, these two bright qualities did not protect the world, then here there would be no recognition of "mother," or "mother's sister," or "maternal uncle's wife," or "teacher's wife," or "the wives of those to be honored." The world would fall into promiscuous confusion, just as goats and sheep, fowl and pigs, dogs and jackals do. But because, monks, these two bright qualities do protect the world, therefore there is recognition of "mother," or "mother's sister," or "maternal uncle's wife," or "teacher's wife," or "the wives of those to be honored." This is the meaning that the Blessed One spoke. And in this connection it is said:

"Those in whom shame and fear of wrongdoing
are never found at all,
have fallen away from the wholesome root,
and are headed for birth and death.
But those in whom shame and fear of wrongdoing
are always rightly established,
grown in the holy life,
are at peace, with renewed becoming destroyed."

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

Thus was it said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "There is, monks, an unborn, an unbecome, an unmade, an unconditioned. If, monks, there were no unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, then there would be no escape discerned here from what is born, become, made, and conditioned. But because, monks, there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, therefore an escape from what is born, become, made, and conditioned is discerned." This is the meaning that the Blessed One spoke. And in this connection it is said:

"What is born, become, arisen,
made, conditioned, and unstable,
this very meaning, bound up [with decay],
a nest of disease, perishable —
it was said that it springs from what is not self,
not fit to be delighted in.
From past kamma comes the peaceful escape,
beyond the sphere of reasoning, enduring —
unarisen, [free from] remorse,
sorrowless, stainless, the [ultimate] state..."

210
Sutta Piṭaka, Khuddaka Nikāya.

"Minds liberated through the exhaustion of the leash to existence,
delighting in the attainment of the essence of the Dhamma at its culmination (the destruction of defilements) —
such steadfast ones have abandoned all states of becoming."

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

Thus was it said by the Blessed One, said by the Worthy One, so I have heard: "Dwell devoted to seclusion, monks, delighting in seclusion; internally devoted to calm of mind, not neglecting absorption (jhāna), endowed with insight, cultivators of empty dwellings. For monks who dwell devoted to seclusion, delighting in seclusion, internally devoted to calm of mind, not neglecting absorption, endowed with insight, cultivators of empty dwellings, one of two fruits may be expected: either final knowledge here and now, or, if there is a remainder of clinging, the state of non-returning."

This meaning the Blessed One spoke. And in this connection it is said:

"Those of peaceful mind, prudent, mindful and meditative,
who rightly see the Dhamma with insight, free from longing for sensual pleasures,
who delight in diligence, are at peace, and see danger in negligence —
such ones are incapable of falling back; they are close indeed to Nibbāna."

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

Thus was it said by the Blessed One, said by the Worthy One, so I have heard: "Dwell, monks, with the benefit of training as your guide, with wisdom supreme, with liberation as the essence, with mindfulness as the governing factor. This meaning the Blessed One spoke. And in this connection it is said:

"One perfected in training, of unfailing virtue,
supreme in wisdom, who sees the ending of birth..."

Itivuttaka, Book of Twos, Second Chapter. 211

That sage, indeed, bearing his final body,
I call one who has abandoned Mara, gone beyond old age.
Therefore, always delighting in meditation, concentrated,
Ardent, seeing the ending of birth,
Having overcome Mara together with his army, monks,
Become those who have crossed beyond birth and death.

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One. Thus have I heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, thus have I heard: "Monks, a monk should dwell wakeful, mindful, clearly comprehending, concentrated, joyful, and serene, and there discern the right time among wholesome states. Monks, for a monk who dwells wakeful, mindful, clearly comprehending, concentrated, joyful, serene, discerning the right time among wholesome states, one of two fruits may be expected: either final knowledge here and now, or, if there is a remainder of clinging, the state of non-returning." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke. And in connection with this, it was said:

"Listen, you who are awake, to this: let those who sleep awaken,
Waking is better than sleeping; for one who is awake there is no fear.

He who is wakeful, mindful, clearly comprehending,
Concentrated, joyful, and serene,
Rightly examining the Dhamma at the proper time,
Being unified in mind, dispels the darkness —
Therefore one should indeed devote oneself to wakefulness.

The ardent monk, wise, who has gained the jhanas,
Having cut off the fetters of birth and old age,
Touches, here itself, unsurpassed enlightenment."

Itivuttaka, Dukanipata, Second Chapter.  213

"This is peaceful, this is excellent, this is just as it truly is" — thus, monks, some go beyond [what is right]. And how, monks, do those with clear eyes see? Here, a monk sees what has come to be as what has come to be; having seen what has come to be as what has come to be, he practices for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation with regard to what has come to be. Thus, monks, do those with clear eyes see. This matter was spoken by the Blessed One; thus it is said:

"He who has seen what has come to be as what has come to be,
And has gone beyond what has come to be,
Is freed in accordance with truth,
Through the exhaustion of craving for existence.
He indeed has fully understood what has come to be,
Free from craving as regards all states of being.
Through the ceasing of what has come to be, O monk,
He does not come again to renewed existence."

This matter too was spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

Beings bound by the yoke of craving, their minds dyed by becoming and non-becoming,

Itivuttaka, Book of Threes, Second Chapter.

Thus it was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, there are these three bases of meritorious action. What three? The basis of merit consisting in giving, the basis of merit consisting in virtue, and the basis of merit consisting in meditation. These, monks, are the three bases of meritorious action." This is the meaning the Blessed One stated. In this regard it is said:

    "One should train in merit alone,
    which brings lasting, happy faculties --
    giving, and a life of virtue,
    and the cultivation of a loving mind.
    Having developed these three things
    that bring about happiness,
    the wise one arises in a happy world,
    free from affliction."

This too is the meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

Thus it was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, there are these three eyes. What three? The fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the eye of wisdom. These, monks, are the three eyes." This is the meaning the Blessed One stated. In this regard it is said:

    "The fleshly eye, the divine eye,
    and the unsurpassed eye of wisdom --
    these three eyes
    were declared by the Supreme Person.
    The arising of the fleshly eye
    is the path to the divine eye;
    from which knowledge arose --
    the unsurpassed eye of wisdom.
    By the attainment of that eye,
    one is released from all suffering."

Thus it was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, there are these three faculties. What three? The faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,' the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known. These, monks, are the three faculties." This is the meaning the Blessed One stated. In this regard it is said:

Itivuttaka, Book of Threes, Second Chapter.

For one still in training, who is practicing the training,
following the straight path,
the first knowledge arises at the moment of destruction [of defilements],
then direct knowledge follows without interval.
Then, for one who is liberated,
such knowledge arises in the one who is steadfast:
"Unshakeable is my liberation,"
through the destruction of the fetters of existence.
Truly, one accomplished in the faculties,
at peace, delighting in the state of peace,
bears his final body,
having conquered Mara together with his mount.

This too is a meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Bhikkhus, there are these three time-periods. What three? The past time, the future time, the present time. These, bhikkhus, are the three time-periods." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke. And concerning this it was said:

"Beings who have the perception of what can be named
are established in what can be named.
Not having fully understood what can be named,
they fall under the yoke of death.
But having fully understood what can be named,
one does not conceive of a 'namer';
for that does not exist for him
by which he could be described — it is not found.
Touched by liberation in mind,
the unsurpassed state of peace —
truly, one accomplished regarding what can be named,
at peace, delighting in the state of peace,
steadfast in the Dhamma, having destroyed [craving],
does not return — being a knower (vedagū)."

This too is a meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of misconduct. What three? Bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of misconduct." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke. And concerning this it was said:

"Having committed bodily misconduct,
and verbal misconduct too,
having committed mental misconduct,
and whatever else is reckoned as faulty,
not having done wholesome deeds,
but having done much that is unwholesome,
at the breaking up of the body, the unwise one
is reborn in hell."

Itivuttaka, Chapter of Threes, Second Division.                    221

"Monks, lust is a shackle, hatred is a shackle, delusion is a shackle. This is called, monks, a bound monk - fastened by Mara's snare, able to be done with as the Wicked One wishes. Whoever, monks, has abandoned lust, abandoned hatred, abandoned delusion - this is called, monks, one unbound, freed from Mara's snare, not able to be done with as the Wicked One wishes." The Blessed One spoke this meaning. Thus it was said:

"One whose lust and hatred
and ignorance are dispelled -
that developed one, a certain Brahma-become,
the Tathagata,
the Buddha who has gone beyond enmity and fear,
is said to have abandoned all."

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One; thus I have heard.

Thus was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Whoever, monks, whether a monk or a nun, has not abandoned lust, has not abandoned hatred, has not abandoned delusion - this one is called, monks, one who has not crossed the ocean with its waves, its whirlpools, its sharks, and its demons. Whoever, monks, whether a monk or a nun, has abandoned lust, abandoned hatred, abandoned delusion - this one is called, monks, one who has crossed the ocean with its waves, its whirlpools, its sharks, and its demons, who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry land - a brahmin." The Blessed One spoke this meaning. Thus it was said:

"One whose lust and hatred
and ignorance are dispelled
has crossed this ocean with its sharks and demons,
its waves and perils so hard to cross;
gone beyond attachment, having abandoned death, without any acquisition,
having given up suffering for the sake of no further becoming,
he has gone to his end - he cannot be measured."

222        Sutta Piṭaka, Khuddaka Nikāya.

"I declare him the vanquisher of delusion, the king of death."
This too is the meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One — thus have I heard.
The Second Chapter, the Second.
Its summary:

Merit, the eye, then the faculty,
Time, conduct, two kinds of happiness,
The sage, then passion, two more,
Thus is told the second chapter, the finest.

In the Itivuttaka, the Third Chapter of the Threes (Tika Nipāta).

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, I have seen beings endowed with bodily misconduct, endowed with verbal misconduct, endowed with mental misconduct, who reviled the Noble Ones, who held wrong view, and who undertook actions based on wrong view. At the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell. Monks, I do not say this having merely heard it from some other ascetic or brahmin: Monks, I have seen beings endowed with bodily misconduct, endowed with verbal misconduct, endowed with mental misconduct, who reviled the Noble Ones, who held wrong view, and who undertook actions based on wrong view. At the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell. Rather, monks, just as I myself have known, seen, and understood it, so do I declare: 'Monks, I have seen beings endowed with bodily misconduct, endowed with verbal misconduct, endowed with mental misconduct, who reviled the Noble Ones, who held wrong view, and who undertook actions based on wrong view. At the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell.'"

224. Sutta Pitaka, Khuddaka Nikaya.

"One who is greatly learned, who performs merit, living with little here in this life — at the breaking up of the body, having gained (merit), he arises in heaven." This too is a meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, there are these three elements leading to release. What three? The release from sensual pleasures, namely renunciation; the release from forms, namely the formless; and whatever has come to be, is conditioned, dependently arisen — cessation is the release from that. These, monks, are the three elements leading to release." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke, and concerning this it was said:

"Having known the release from sensual desire, and the transcending of forms,
Touching the stilling of all formations, ever ardent,
That monk who rightly perceives is thereby released,
Accomplished through direct knowledge, at peace, having gone beyond bondage — he is a sage."
This too is a meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, the formless states are more peaceful than forms; cessation is more peaceful than the formless states." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke, and concerning this it was said:

"Those beings who cling to form, and those who dwell in the formless,
Not understanding cessation, come again to renewed existence.
But those who have fully understood forms, and are not fixed in the formless,
Those who are released in cessation — those people have left death behind.
Having touched with the body the deathless element, free of acquisitions,
Having realized the relinquishing of acquisitions, free of taints,
The Perfectly Enlightened One teaches the sorrowless, stainless path."

Itivuttaka, Third Chapter of the Threes.

This too is the meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One; so I have heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, there are these three kinds of sons found existing in the world. What three? The son who surpasses (his parents), the son who is like (his parents), and the son who falls short (of his parents).

And how, monks, does a son become one who surpasses (his parents)? Here, monks, a son's parents have not gone for refuge to the Buddha, have not gone for refuge to the Dhamma, have not gone for refuge to the Sangha; they do not abstain from killing living beings, do not abstain from taking what is not given, do not abstain from sexual misconduct, do not abstain from false speech, do not abstain from the ground of heedlessness through liquor and intoxicants; they are unvirtuous, of bad character. But their son has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, gone for refuge to the Sangha; he abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, abstains from the ground of heedlessness through liquor and intoxicants; he is virtuous, of good character. Thus, monks, does a son become one who surpasses (his parents).

And how, monks, does a son become one who is like (his parents)? Here, monks, a son's parents have gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, gone for refuge to the Sangha; they abstain from killing living beings, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from the ground of heedlessness through liquor and intoxicants; they are virtuous, of good character. And their son too has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, gone for refuge to the Sangha; he abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, abstains from the ground of heedlessness through liquor and intoxicants; he is virtuous, of good character. Thus, monks, does a son become one who is like (his parents)."

226                Suttanta Pitaka, Khuddaka Nikaya.

"And how, monks, is a son unworthy (not nobly born)? Here, monks, a son's parents have gone to the Buddha for refuge, gone to the Dhamma for refuge, gone to the Sangha for refuge; they abstain from killing living beings, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from the heedlessness that comes from fermented and distilled liquors; they are virtuous, of good character. But their son is not so: he has not gone to the Buddha for refuge, has not gone to the Dhamma for refuge, has not gone to the Sangha for refuge; he does not abstain from killing living beings, does not abstain from taking what is not given, does not abstain from sexual misconduct, does not abstain from false speech, does not abstain from the heedlessness that comes from fermented and distilled liquors; he is of bad virtue, evil in nature. Thus, monks, is a son unworthy. These, monks, are the three kinds of sons that exist and are found in the world."

This matter was spoken by the Blessed One. Here it is said:

"The wise wish for a son who surpasses or equals [his parents];
they do not wish for an unworthy son who disgraces the family.
These are the true sons in the world —
those who become lay devotees,
endowed with faith and virtue,
generous, free from stinginess,
shining among the assemblies
like the moon freed from clouds."

This too is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.

Thus was it said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "There are, monks, three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The one who rains nowhere, the one who rains in some places, and the one who rains everywhere.

"And how, monks, is one a person who rains nowhere? Here, monks, a certain person gives nothing at all — he does not give food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, lodging, or lamps to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, beggars, or wanderers. Thus, monks, is such a person one who rains nowhere."

228                    Suttanta Pitaka   Khuddaka Nikaya.

This too is the meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

Thus it was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, established in three kinds of benefit, a wise person should guard virtue (sila). What are the three? 'May praise come to me' — for this a wise person should guard virtue. 'May wealth arise for me' — for this a wise person should guard virtue. 'At the breaking up of the body after death, I will arise in a good destination, a heavenly world' — for this a wise person should guard virtue. These, monks, are the three benefits, established in which a wise person should guard virtue." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke. And in this connection it is said:

A wise person should guard virtue,
as the foundation of three kinds of happiness:
praise, the gaining of wealth,
and after death, rejoicing in heaven.

Even one who does no evil himself,
if he keeps company with one who does evil,
becomes suspected of evil,
and a bad reputation grows upon him.

Whatever kind of friend one keeps,
whatever kind one associates with,
such indeed one becomes oneself,
for such is the nature of companionship.

One who associates with another who is tainted
becomes touched by that taint himself,
like a quiver contaminated
by a poisoned arrow placed within it.

Fearing such contamination, the wise
should never become a companion to the wicked.

If a man wraps rotten fish in grass,
the grass too becomes foul-smelling —
so it is with association with fools.

But if a man wraps fragrant powder in a leaf,
the leaf too becomes fragrant —
so it is with association with the wise.

Therefore, knowing his own nature
to be like a leaf used for wrapping,
a wise person should not associate with the bad,
but should associate with the good.
The bad lead one to hell,
the good lead one to a good destination.

Itivuttaka, the Threefold Book, Third Chapter.    229

This too is a meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "This body, monks, is breaking apart; consciousness is of a nature to fade away; all acquisitions are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change." This is the meaning the Blessed One declared. And in this connection it was said:

    "Knowing the body as something that is breaking apart,
    and consciousness as something that crumbles away,
    having seen the danger in acquisitions,
    one who has overcome birth and death,
    one of developed self, awaits the time [of death],
    [having reached] the highest peace."

This too is a meaning spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard: "Monks, beings come together and associate according to their dispositions: beings of base disposition come together and associate with beings of base disposition; beings of good disposition come together and associate with beings of good disposition. In the past too, monks, in time gone by, beings came together and associated according to their dispositions: beings of base disposition came together and associated with beings of base disposition; beings of good disposition came together and associated with beings of good disposition. In the future too, monks, in time to come, beings will come together and associate according to their dispositions: beings of base disposition will come together and associate with beings of base disposition; beings of good disposition will come together and associate with beings of good disposition. Now also, monks, in the present time, beings come together and associate according to their dispositions: beings of base disposition come together and associate with beings of base disposition; beings of good disposition come together and associate with beings of good disposition." This is the meaning the Blessed One declared. And in this connection it was said:

    "From association, entanglement is born;
    by non-association, it is cut off..."

230          Sutta Piṭaka. Khuddaka Nikāya.

"Just as one who climbs onto a small piece of wood
sinks in the great ocean,
so too, by associating with the lazy,
even one who lives a good life sinks.
Therefore one should avoid
the lazy one of poor energy;
one should dwell together with secluded noble ones,
resolute, meditative,
ever of aroused energy,
with the wise."

This too is the meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Worthy One, so I have heard: "Monks, there are two things that lead to the decline of a monk in training. What two? Here, monks, a monk in training delights in work, takes pleasure in work, is devoted to delighting in work; delights in talk, takes pleasure in talk, is devoted to delighting in talk; delights in sleep, takes pleasure in sleep, is devoted to delighting in sleep. These, monks, are the two things that lead to the decline of a monk in training.

Monks, there are two things that lead to the non-decline of a monk in training. What two? Here, monks, a monk in training does not delight in work, does not take pleasure in work, is not devoted to delighting in work; does not delight in talk, does not take pleasure in talk, is not devoted to delighting in talk; does not delight in sleep, does not take pleasure in sleep, is not devoted to delighting in sleep. These, monks, are the two things that lead to the non-decline of a monk in training."

This is the meaning that the Blessed One spoke. In this connection it is said:

"One who delights in work, takes pleasure in talk,
and delights in sleep, being restless—
such a monk is incapable
of attaining the supreme enlightenment.
Therefore, one with few duties,
not drowsy, not restless—
such a monk is capable
of attaining the supreme enlightenment."

This too is the meaning that was spoken by the Blessed One, so I have heard.

The third chapter, the third [sutta].

232                    In the Sutta Piṭaka, Khuddaka Nikāya.

"Monks, I have seen beings overcome and overwhelmed in mind by disrespect, who, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in a lower realm, in hell. I have also seen, monks, beings overcome and overwhelmed in mind by both honor and disrespect together, who, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in a lower realm, in hell.

Moreover, monks, as for what I myself have known, seen, and understood, this is what I declare: I have seen beings overcome and overwhelmed in mind by honor, who are reborn in hell as described; I have seen beings overcome and overwhelmed in mind by disrespect, who are likewise reborn in hell; and I have seen beings overcome and overwhelmed in mind by both honor and disrespect together, who are likewise reborn in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in a lower realm, in hell."

    "For one who is honored, and likewise for one treated with disrespect,
    whose concentration does not waver, who dwells heedfully --
    him, the meditator, the steadfast one, who sees subtly through insight,
    who delights in the ending of clinging -- him they call a true person."

"Monks, there are these three divine proclamations that resound among the gods, each arising on its proper occasion. What three? Monks, at the time when a noble disciple decides to shave off hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness, at that time a divine proclamation resounds among the gods: 'This noble disciple has resolved to do battle with Māra.' This, monks, is the first divine proclamation that resounds among the gods on its proper occasion.

Furthermore, monks, at the time when a noble disciple [cultivates] the seven qualities that are factors of enlightenment..."

233

"...devoted to the practice of meditation. At that time, monks, a divine sound arises among the gods, saying: 'This noble disciple is doing battle together with Mara.' This, monks, is the second divine sound that arises among the gods, from time to time.

Furthermore, monks, at the time when a noble disciple, through the destruction of the taints, having realized it for himself by direct knowledge here and now, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, at that time, monks, a divine sound arises among the gods, saying: 'This noble disciple, having won the battle, dwells having conquered that very battlefront.' This, monks, is the third divine sound that arises among the gods, from time to time.

These, monks, are the three divine sounds that arise among the gods, from time to time."

Having seen the one who has won the battle, the disciple of the Fully Self-Awakened One,
Even the deities pay homage to that great one, free from fear.
Homage to you, excellent among men, who have overcome what is hard to conquer,
Having defeated the army of Death, through liberation unobstructed.
Thus the deities pay homage to one who has attained the goal of his mind;
They pay homage to him by whom the power of Death has been overcome.

Just as, monks, when a god is subject to passing away from the company of the gods, five foretokens appear to him: his garlands wither, his garments become soiled, sweat issues from his armpits, an unpleasant hue appears on his body, and the god takes no delight in his heavenly seat — then, monks, the other gods, knowing "this god is subject to passing away," console him with three sayings: "Good sir, go from here to a happy destination. Having gone to a happy destination, obtain a good gain. Having obtained a good gain, be well established."

...for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. What three? Here, bhikkhus, a Tathagata arises in the world — an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, Fortunate One, Knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he proclaims the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. This, bhikkhus, is the first person who, arising in the world, arises for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a disciple of that very teacher is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through right knowledge. He too teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he proclaims the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. This too, bhikkhus, is the second person who, arising in the world, arises for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a disciple of that very teacher is a trainee (sekha), one who has entered the path, who is learned, endowed with virtue and observances. He too teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he proclaims the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. This too, bhikkhus, is the third person who, arising in the world, arises for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

These, bhikkhus, are the three persons who, arising in the world, arise for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
